title: Class diagrams for LLD
idea: A class diagram is a map of your design's types: each box names a class with its fields and methods, and each line shows how two classes connect.
points: Each class box has three parts: name, attributes, then operations with return types.
Visibility marks: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected, `~` package-private.
An arrow with multiplicity like 1 to 0..* usually becomes a field or collection.
In interviews, sketch boxes and arrows first; add members only for the core classes.

steps.caption: Start with one box. `Library` lists private fields under its name, then public operations with return types.
The «interface» stereotype marks a contract. `LoanPolicy` has operations only, no state.
A dashed line with a hollow triangle is realisation. `StudentPolicy` implements `LoanPolicy`.
A solid arrow is an association. `Library` holds exactly one policy, so the far end reads 1.
Multiplicity 0..* means zero or more. In Java that becomes a `List` field.
Each `Loan` points at one `Book` and one `Member`. Arrowheads show who knows whom.

code.title: The diagram
code.caption: The same design as Mermaid text. Paste it into any Mermaid viewer to draw it.

walk.text: A class block: `-` private attributes first, then `+` operations with their return type last.
The `<<interface>>` stereotype marks a contract with no state.
`<|..` draws the dashed realisation line from implementation to interface.
Quoted text near each end is multiplicity: how many objects sit at that end.
Arrowheads show direction: a `Loan` knows its book and member, not the reverse.

code.title: The code it maps to
code.caption: Every box is a type and every solid arrow is a field. The rules the diagram hides live in methods.

walk.text: The interface and its implementation match the dashed realisation line one to one.
Records give private final fields, the `-` attributes in the boxes.
Each association arrow from `Library` becomes one private final field; 0..* becomes a list.
The policy is injected through the constructor, so swapping `StudentPolicy` needs no edit to `Library`.
Rules such as loan limits are not drawn. They live in `lend` and fail loudly.
Return a copy so callers cannot change the 0..* collection behind the diagram's back.

pitfalls: Drawing every getter and setter buries the design; show only members that explain behaviour.
Drawing realisation with a solid line makes it read as inheritance; dash it.
Leaving out multiplicity makes a list look like a single field; label both ends.

quiz.q: `StudentPolicy` joins `LoanPolicy` with a dashed line and hollow triangle. Which Java matches?
options: A method takes LoanPolicy as a parameter
quiz.why: A dashed line with a hollow triangle is realisation: a class implementing an interface. A solid line with that triangle is inheritance; plain arrows are associations.

takeaway: Boxes are types, solid arrows are fields, numbers are how many.
